title: Chapter 2 – Counting Years
html:
[Lin Clan – Patriarch Lin Zhenshan]

There are forty steps beneath Green Pine Hill, and Lin Zhenshan has counted every one of them every morning for fifty-one years.

The first ten are cold, cut through the pale rock under the stone hut at the top of the hill. By the twentieth the air thickens. By the thirtieth it is warm and heavy and sweet, like breath in a closed room, and by the fortieth step a man who has never cultivated can feel his skin prickle. The chamber at the bottom is no larger than a farmhouse kitchen. A stone basin sits in its center over the place where the vein comes closest to the surface, and the water in the basin glows faintly green, like moonlight through pine needles.

He sits on the worn cushion, straightens his back with the care of a man whose back no longer straightens easily, and begins the Green Pine Breathing Method.

In for eight. Hold for four. Out for eight.

The Qi comes up out of the basin like mist off a warm lake and settles into him, and he guides it down through the channels his grandfather taught him, around the great circuit, and into the dantian below his navel. There, it joins the rest: fifty-one years of refining at the ninth and highest layer of Qi Refining, compressed and polished until it sits in him like a pond of liquid jade.

It is full. It has been full for decades. And it will not change into what it must become.

Foundation Establishment. The step that turns a Qi Refining cultivator, however strong, into something of a different kind. Lifespan doubles. Spiritual sense becomes a true sense. Qi solidifies into a foundation that can carry real spells, real artifacts, a sword that flies. Every clan in this county with a Foundation Establishment elder sits safe behind his name. Every clan without one is waiting to be eaten.

He tried at sixty-eight, with a Foundation Establishment Pill bought from the Azure Cloud Sect with every stone the clan had saved for twenty years. Three meridians tore. Four years to heal. He tried again at ninety-four without a pill, because there was no money for one, and tore two more. Two years.

He is a hundred and ten now. His teacher's teacher used to say that a man gets three chances at the Foundation, and the third one either makes him or kills him.

He has done the arithmetic. Without help, the third attempt will kill him.

He will make it anyway, when the time comes. There is no one else.

He finishes the cycle, opens his eyes, and sits for a while in the green glow, looking at the far wall where the chamber narrows to a single dark step below the rest, the fortieth, black and smooth and unworn. He does not look at it long. He never does.

Then he climbs back up into the morning, because he has a granddaughter to meet.

\ \ \*

The child comes a month early, at dusk, in the middle of a storm of hail that rattles the roof tiles like thrown gravel.

Lin Wenqing delivers her. His daughter has the steadiest hands in the clan and the least patience; she chases her elder brother Wenyuan out of the room twice and then calls him back in when it is over. When Lin Zhenshan enters, the hail has stopped, and his daughter-in-law Su Qinghe is sitting up against the bolsters with a small, red, furious bundle at her breast, and Wenqing is wiping her hands, her own palms still glowing faintly green with the healing art she has just used to close the worst of the tearing.

"A girl," Wenqing says. "Small, but loud. She'll live."

Lin Zhenshan looks down at his granddaughter's crumpled face and feels the thing he always feels at these moments, which is not quite joy and not quite fear. Another life on the hill. Another life to hold.

There is a moon rising over the eastern terraces, huge and pale after the storm. "Yue," he says. "For the moon."

Su Qinghe nods without taking her eyes off the child.

Then, because it is the custom, and because he would rather know now, he takes the Root-Seeking Jade from inside his robe.

It is a cracked green disc the width of his palm, left by his grandfather, Lin Shoucheng. It cannot say what kind of spiritual root a child carries, or how strong; that waits for the full test on the Root Stele at six. But it can say whether there is anything there at all. Laid on a newborn's chest, it glows if there is a root.

For Lin Feng, nine years ago, it blazed like a lantern. Three elements, wood and fire and earth, the best root the family has seen in a century. For Lin Jian, three years ago, it flickered, a weak, uncertain light that came and went like a candle in a draft. Poor. But present.

He lays it on his granddaughter's chest.

Nothing.

He waits. He counts twenty breaths. The jade lies dark and cold against the child's skin.

Su Qinghe's face does not change. She has seen a great deal in her life, Lin Zhenshan's daughter-in-law, ten years as a rogue cultivator in the Beast Mountains before she married his son, and she does not show what she feels in front of people. But her arms tighten around the baby, very slightly.

He picks up the jade. "She is a Lin," he says. "Root or no root."

Later, alone in the clan library, he takes down the family register, a thick book bound in faded blue cloth, and writes beneath the line for Lin Yue in his careful, old-fashioned hand: Spiritual root: none.

The brush hovers a moment longer. Then he sets it down.

When he leaves the library, he finds his three-year-old grandson Lin Jian standing in the corridor outside his mother's room in a nightshirt, looking at the closed door with an expression of intense concentration.

"Little builder," he says. "You should be asleep."

"Sister," the boy says.

"Yes. You have a sister. You'll meet her in the morning."

But in the morning, Su Qinghe tells him that Lin Jian crept into the room before dawn, climbed up onto the bed, put one small finger into the baby's fist, and then went so white that she thought he was ill. He slept until noon.

Lin Zhenshan files this away with the other small strange things he has noticed about his second grandson, and goes to prepare for the Zhao.

\ \ \*

Preparing, for a patriarch, mostly means counting.

He does it at breakfast, the morning before the Zhao are due, while the household eats rice porridge and pickled radish in the long dining room off the kitchen. He has done it every morning for fifty years, the way a farmer looks at the sky. Forty-one people of Lin blood live on the hill. Twelve of them can cultivate. He counts those twelve the way he would count soldiers.

Himself: ninth layer, peak, a hundred and ten, and the only one of them who could stand against a Foundation Establishment cultivator for longer than a few breaths.

His eldest surviving son, Wenyuan, at the end of the table, eating with his right hand while his left lies in his lap. Fifth layer, once, and rising fast. Seven years ago a third-rank shadow lynx came down out of the Beast Mountains and opened him from shoulder to hip in the time it took to blink, and the claw tore four of the primary channels on his left side. He lived. The channels did not heal. He still holds the fifth layer, after a fashion, but his Qi leaks out of him like water from a cracked jar, and in a fight he would do well to match a man of the second. He has made himself the clan's talisman master instead, sitting up half the night with his brush, because a talisman holds Qi that its maker put there yesterday, and a cracked jar can still fill a cup if it is patient. Half of what the family earns comes from his desk. He has never once complained in Lin Zhenshan's hearing. Lin Zhenshan is not sure whether that makes him proud or afraid.

Su Qinghe beside him, the baby asleep in a sling across her chest. Third layer, she tells people; fourth, Lin Zhenshan suspects. A three-element root: water first, then metal, then a little wood. She came up the Willow Ford road eleven years ago with a short bow and a knife and a bounty on the head of the man she had just killed, and Wenyuan married her over his father's objection. Lin Zhenshan was wrong about her. He has never said so. He has noticed that she sits with her back to the wall, that she knows the Beast Mountains better than any hunter in the village, and that the water dart she can throw from her fingertips will go through a plank at forty paces.

His second son, Wenhai: sixth layer, a fire-and-earth dual root, the strongest of his children and the cleverest with money. He is talking pleasantly to the cousin beside him about the price of salt.

His daughter, Wenqing: fourth layer, a four-element root with wood strongest, widowed young when her husband fell from the north cliffs gathering frostbell moss. She runs the herb terraces and the little pill room behind the kitchen where she brews the clan's Breath-Gathering Pills and Hundred-Herb Pills in a bronze cauldron older than she is. Her pills are not good, by Sect standards. They are the only pills the family can afford. She calls rain over the herb beds every dawn with water-gathering talismans her brother draws for her, and she can bind a wild boar in a net of green Qi threads long enough for the hunters to reach it. Her son, Lin Bo, is ten, and first layer, and at this moment is sliding his last rice ball onto Lin Feng's plate when he thinks no one is looking.

His youngest son, Wenshi: fifth layer, a four-element root with metal strongest, thirty years old, the plainest and steadiest of the four. He commands the hill's guard: thirty village men, farmers by day, who train every second morning with the mortal-grade swords and arm-guards the clan buys from the Willow Ford refiners. The arm-guards raise a thin barrier at a drop of blood and a word. The swords carry an edge of Qi a farmer can feed with a little practice. Against a beast or a bandit, thirty such men behind a wall are worth a great deal. Against a cultivator of the sixth layer, they are worth very little. Wenshi knows this. It is why he never sleeps more than five hours.

Then the side branches. Lin Mao, the gray-bearded cousin who teaches the children, sixth layer since he was forty, a four-element root with earth strongest, a fine teacher and a bad leg. Three young cousins of the second and third layers. Lin Feng, nine, second layer, the bright hope of the whole family, already practicing the spear forms with a borrowed shaft in the yard every evening. And Wenhai's son, Lin Hu, five years old and loud, who will be tested in a year.

Twelve. Thirteen, if a child with a flicker of a root ever learns to use it.

He looks down the table at his grandson Lin Jian, who is sitting between his mother and Lin Bo, eating porridge with the grave, methodical care of a man doing surgery. The boy catches him looking and looks back. Then he goes on eating.

Twelve cultivators. One aging ninth-layer patriarch. A vein that is weaker every year, though no one says so aloud. Against a neighbor with a Foundation Establishment elder, a second-grade spirit vein and forty cultivators of his own.

It is not a good count. It has not been a good count for a long time.

He finishes his porridge and goes to get dressed for the Zhao.

\ \ \*

They arrive nine days later, on spirit horses.

Lin Wenshi meets them at the gate. His youngest son has the clan's thirty village guards drawn up in two lines along the gate road, spears grounded, bronze arm-guards polished, the shimmer of their protective charms flickering faintly over each man as they stand to attention. It is meant as courtesy. It is also meant to be counted.

Zhao Heng counts it. Lin Zhenshan, watching from the steps of the main hall, sees him do it, a glance down one line and up the other, pleasant and unhurried.

The Patriarch of the Zhao family of Red Ridge is a hundred and eighty years old and looks sixty: iron-gray hair, a broad, pleasant face, the easy stance of a man who has not been afraid of anyone in this county for a very long time. He reached Foundation Establishment at sixty-one, the first of his line. His Qi does not press on the courtyard the way a Foundation Establishment cultivator's usually does. It lies quiet and folded, like a sleeping dog, and Lin Zhenshan knows that this is a choice. There is a small bronze incense burner hanging from Zhao Heng's belt, and a thread of gray smoke curls from it that smells of nothing at all.

Two grandsons ride behind him, a boy of nine and a younger one, and four servants with gifts. Silk. A jade comb for the new mother. Tonics in sealed bottles. And, last, presented by Zhao Heng himself with both hands, a bundle of incense wrapped in white paper.

"From the Cloud Mist Temple," he says. "The finest in the province. I heard about the little one. And I thought, Brother Lin, that at our age it does no harm to offer condolences in advance."

White is the color of mourning.

Behind Lin Zhenshan, someone draws a sharp breath. He thinks it is Wenshi.

Lin Zhenshan takes the incense with both hands and bows exactly as deeply as courtesy requires. "Brother Zhao is very thoughtful."

They drink tea in the main hall. The grandsons are sent to look at the koi pond with Lin Feng, who is nine and at the second layer of Qi Refining and does not hide his dislike of either of them. The elder Zhao boy, Zhao Qian, is already at the fourth layer at nine, and does not hide that either.

Halfway through the second pot, a sharp crack comes from the courtyard, then a hiss, then Lin Feng's voice raised in fury. Lin Zhenshan does not turn his head. Through the open doors he can see well enough: a koi floating belly-up in the pond with a smoking hole through its back, Zhao Qian lowering two fingers with a small flame still guttering on their tips, and Lin Feng, two years younger and a head shorter, with both fists clenched and his face white.

"It was an accident," Zhao Qian says, loudly enough to be heard in the hall. "The fish moved."

Lin Feng says nothing. He looks at the hall doors, at his grandfather, and Lin Zhenshan meets his eyes for one heartbeat and gives the smallest shake of his head. The boy's fists open. He turns his back on the Zhao boy and walks away to the far side of the pond, and he stays there, rigid, until it is time for the guests to go.

"Children," says Zhao Heng comfortably, and refills his own cup.

"Children," Lin Zhenshan agrees.

He will remember the hole in the fish. It was very small and very clean. A Solar Wheel spark from a fourth-layer boy should not be that precise. Someone has been teaching Zhao Qian to aim.

Zhao Heng talks about the weather. The rice harvest. The new deacon the Azure Cloud Sect has sent to collect this year's tribute. He is very pleasant. He has always been pleasant. In a hundred years of neighborliness, Lin Zhenshan cannot remember one unpleasant word from the man.

That is the problem with Zhao Heng.

A Foundation Establishment elder could walk up this hill on any morning he chose and kill every cultivator on it before lunch. Lin Zhenshan is the strongest man on Green Pine Hill, and against Zhao Heng he would last perhaps twenty exchanges. They both know it.

But Zhao Heng will not walk up the hill. The Lin Clan pays tribute to the Azure Cloud Sect, and so do the Zhao, and the Sect's Vassal Compact is very old and very clear: tributary families do not raise their hands against one another. Their quarrels go to the Outer Affairs Hall, to be weighed by Sect arbiters. An elder who kills a tributary patriarch does not keep his family's seat in the Sect's outer court, or its trade rights, or, if the Enforcement Hall is in a bad mood, his head. The Sect does not care about the Lin Clan. It cares a great deal about its tribute, and about a world in which its vassals do not burn one another's fields.

So Zhao Heng comes with silk and tonics and white-wrapped incense. He comes with offers to lease the eastern terraces, and loans at kind rates, and talisman prices cut below cost in every county town within a day's ride. He comes like a merchant, because a merchant is the only thing the Compact lets him be.

And he waits for Lin Zhenshan to die.

"I hear," Zhao Heng says, setting down his cup, "that the tribute has been difficult this year."

"Every year is difficult."

"Of course." Zhao Heng smiles. "Still. Thirty stones is not such a large sum between neighbors. If Brother Lin would allow me—"

Lin Zhenshan does not move. He has had a hundred and ten years to learn how not to move.

"That is generous," he says. "But the Lin Clan will manage."

"Of course," says Zhao Heng again, and talks about the weather.

\ \ \*

When the Zhao have gone, Lin Zhenshan sits alone in the main hall with a cold cup of tea and the white-wrapped incense on the table in front of him, and thinks about the number thirty.

The real shortfall is twenty-six.

He knows, because he counted the treasury himself on the night of the last council. And then, the morning after, he did something he has never done before in his life. He called each member of the council to him privately, one by one, on different pretexts, and to each of them he mentioned the shortfall in passing.

To Wenqing, he said twenty-four. To Wenshi, twenty-seven. To Wenyuan, twenty-two. To his son Wenhai, who keeps the accounts and could have counted it for himself and did not, he said thirty.

He had hoped, with the part of him that is still a father, to hear none of the numbers again.

He sits for a long time.

It is not proof. It is his word about a private conversation, and his word against his son's. Under Lin law, a traitor is judged by the full council of the clan, every adult of the main line and the side branches, before witnesses, on proof. That law was written by Lin Shoucheng himself, after a cousin of his was killed on a rumor, and it has held the family together for a hundred and fifty years. A patriarch who breaks it to punish his own son on a private suspicion breaks the clan with it.

And Wenhai is not alone. Lin Zhenshan knows, the way he knows the weather, that his second son has spent ten years lending small sums out of the clan's accounts to five of the side-branch households: a roof repaired here, a dowry there, a debt quietly forgiven. Half the cultivators in the side branches owe Wenhai something. Accuse him without proof, and they will stand with him out of fear for their own debts. Then there are two clans on Green Pine Hill, and neither one can hold it.

And there is Zhao Heng, who would like nothing better than to carry a petition to the Outer Affairs Hall saying that the old tyrant of Green Pine Hill has begun killing his own sons, and asking the Sect to appoint an arbiter to see the hill properly governed.

Lin Zhenshan looks at the incense.

He is old, and tired, and in the arithmetic of years he is nearly out of time. But he is not stupid. His grandfather used to say the Lins kept the sword and lost the mind, that they had grown too proud for cunning. Perhaps that is true. Perhaps it is time to remember.

A leak you know about is not only a wound. It is also a door. Whatever goes into Wenhai's ears comes out at Red Ridge. And Zhao Heng, for all his patience, will believe what comes out at Red Ridge.

Very well, my son, he thinks. Let us see what you carry for me.

He picks up the white-wrapped incense and goes to put it on the highest shelf in the hall, where it will sit unopened for as long as he lives. As he reaches up, he catches a movement at the edge of his vision and turns.

Behind the folding screen at the side of the hall, where the household's youngest children are sometimes put to nap during long councils, there is a gap where the third hinge is torn. Through that gap a small face is watching. Not him. His son Wenhai, who has just come into the hall from the side door with an account book under his arm and a pleasant expression.

The face behind the screen belongs to Lin Jian. The boy is three years old, and his eyes, fixed on his uncle, are as cold and steady as Zhao Heng's.

Lin Zhenshan looks at his grandson for a long moment.

Then he goes on putting the incense on the shelf, and says nothing at all.

\ \ \*

That evening, he does something else he has not done in years. He goes down to the gate yard, where Wenshi is drilling the village guards by lamplight, and asks for a sword.

His youngest son stares at him, then hands him a practice blade. The guards draw back to the edges of the yard and stand very still.

Lin Zhenshan has not drawn steel in public in twenty years. He holds the blade loosely for a moment, feeling the weight, and then he moves into the first form of the Green Pine Sword Art. Pine in Wind. The blade sweeps, low and patient. Second form, Root and Stone: he plants his feet and the Qi drops through him into the packed earth, and the ground under the yard hums. Third form, Needles in Rain. The blade flickers, and on the far side of the yard three lamp flames go out one after another, cut from their wicks by arcs of silver Qi he never seems to aim.

He stops. He is breathing harder than he would like.

"Father," Wenshi says quietly.

"Practice with them every day from now on," Lin Zhenshan says, handing back the sword. "Not every second day. Every day. Teach them the mantle charms until they can raise them in their sleep. And teach Feng the spear forms himself, not only the side-branch cousins." He looks around at the yard, at the village men in their bronze arm-guards, at his son's broad, worried face. "We have been a quiet family for a long time. It's time we became a careful one."

He walks back up the hill alone in the dark, counting his steps out of habit, and does not let himself think about how many of them he has left.

At the top, outside the main hall, the screen with the torn hinge stands folded against the wall. He stops beside it for a moment, touches the torn hinge with one finger, and wonders what a child of three sees when he looks at a man like that.

Then he goes inside to sleep, and for once, he dreams of nothing at all.
